title: Nduanu — the porridge
description: Ide hot pot potatoes: nduanu = nduko (potato) + anu (meat).
html:
Nduanu Ide Hot Pot Potatoes Serves 5–6 Inspiration / Origin Inspired by: Cameroonian hot pot potatoes. Introduction Nduanu takes its name from potato (nduko) and meat (anu). The potatoes are parboiled and then fried until crisp, the protein is boiled and then fried separately, and both are folded into a properly built tomato-vegetable gravy at the end — always with boneless protein, whether that's chicken, beef, cow tongue, tozo, or turkey. Recipe Information Serves: 5–6 Preparation time: 25 minutes Cooking time: about 1 hour (boneless turkey); 1.5–2 hours for cow tongue Total time: 1 hour 25 minutes (boneless turkey); longer for cow tongue Ingredients Main Irish potatoes, peeled Carrots, sliced Green beans, chopped Bell peppers, sliced Protein — NO BONES, EVER. Beef tongue, store-cleaned and cubed — the signature meat or turkey, boneless — the outer and edge parts, never the thick inside of the breast No animal used in nduanu may have a bone in it, and no cut with a bone is substituted for one without. Vegetables & Aromatics Onions Tomatoes Garlic Fresh ginger Fat & Seasoning Vegetable oil, for deep-frying Curry powder White pepper Seasoning cubes Salt Equipment Pot for parboiling and boiling Deep frying pan Separate clean pot for the gravy Chopping board and knife Preparation 1. Peel the Irish potatoes, slicing very large ones in half and keeping medium ones whole. 2. Rinse the chosen protein thoroughly. It must be boneless: the signature meat is beef tongue, store-cleaned and ready to cube directly with no further peeling; otherwise boneless turkey, using the outer and edge parts and not the thick inside of the breast. 3. Slice the carrots, chop the green beans, and slice the bell peppers. Cooking Method 1. Parboil the potatoes in salted water with a pinch of curry powder for about 8 to 15 minutes, until they're slightly softened on the outside but still firm enough that they won't break apart later. Drain and set aside. 2. Boil the chosen protein with chopped onion, garlic, ginger, salt and a seasoning cube until completely tender. Chicken, beef, and turkey take about 1 hour; cow tongue needs 1.5–2 hours even when store-cleaned, since the cut is naturally dense. Remove the meat from the pot and set it aside, but keep the rich stock — it becomes the base of the gravy later. 3. Heat vegetable oil in a deep frying pan. Fry the boiled protein until golden brown and dry on the outside, then set it aside. In the exact same oil, deep-fry the parboiled potatoes until they develop a golden-brown, crispy crust, then remove them as well. 4. In a separate clean pot, heat a few tablespoons of oil and fry chopped onions and tomatoes until all the water has evaporated and the raw sourness of the tomato is gone. 5. Stir in the garlic, ginger, white pepper and the remaining curry powder. Pour in a little of the reserved meat stock to build a thick gravy, then add the carrots, green beans and bell peppers, letting them simmer for about 3 minutes for a crisp-tender bite — extend to 5–6 minutes if you prefer the vegetables softer. 6. Taste the gravy and adjust the salt before adding the protein and potatoes, since the stock's saltiness varies depending on how much it has reduced. 7. Gently fold the fried protein and the crispy fried potatoes into the bubbling vegetable sauce, stirring carefully so the potatoes stay whole rather than breaking apart. 8. Reduce the heat to low, cover the pot tightly, and let everything simmer together for 7 to 10 minutes so the potatoes absorb the aromatic flavours of the gravy without losing their crisp-tender texture. Chef's Notes Even store-cleaned boneless protein is worth a quick visual check for any small bone fragments before it goes into the pot — this is a strict rule for this dish. Fry the protein and the potatoes in the same oil, in that order, so the potatoes pick up a little of the meat's flavour. Stir gently once the potatoes are in the gravy; the goal is coating them, not breaking them down. Variations Cow tongue — the richest, most traditional version; store-cleaned tongue needs no extra prep, just a longer 1.5–2 hour boil for tenderness Turkey — a lighter, quicker pot Tozo — the most prestigious version Serving Suggestions Serve hot as a complete stew, no swallow required Good with fresh bread or plain rice on the side Appearance Crisp, golden potato pieces holding their shape in a thick red-orange gravy Visible carrot, green bean and bell pepper throughout Flavour Profile Warm and earthy with a gentle curry depth Crisp-edged potato against a rich, tender protein Fresh lift from the vegetables Nutritional Highlights Good source of potassium and vitamin C from the potato Balanced protein from the chosen meat Carrots add vitamin A Cultural Significance Nduanu brings a well-loved Cameroonian home-style dish into Ide cuisine, refined around a strict no-bone standard and a proper two-stage cooking method — boiled then fried, for both the potato and the protein — so it can be served with full confidence at any family or festival table.
